facts: The Sun contains 99.86% of all the mass in our Solar System.
About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside the Sun's volume.
Core temperatures reach roughly 15 million degrees Celsius, driving nuclear fusion.
Every second, the Sun fuses about 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to Earth.
A photon created in the Sun's core can take over 100,000 years to reach the surface.
The Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, is paradoxically hotter than its visible surface.
The Sun rotates faster at its equator (25 days) than at its poles (35 days).
It is a G-type main-sequence star, roughly 4.6 billion years old.
The solar wind carves out a giant magnetic bubble called the heliosphere.
Sunspots are cooler, magnetically intense regions that cycle every 11 years.
In about 5 billion years, the Sun will expand into a red giant.
Mercury is the smallest planet in the Solar System, barely larger than Earth's Moon.
A single solar day on Mercury (sunrise to sunrise) lasts 176 Earth days—twice its year.
Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury is not the hottest planet; Venus is.
Surface temperatures swing from 430°C in daylight to -180°C at night.
Mercury has a massive iron core making up about 85% of the planet's radius.
Permanently shadowed craters at Mercury's poles contain water ice.
It has an ultra-thin exosphere rather than a true atmosphere.
The Caloris Basin is one of the largest impact craters in the Solar System at 1,550 km wide.
Mercury is slowly shrinking as its iron core cools, forming giant cliffs called scarps.
It orbits the Sun faster than any other planet at nearly 47 km per second.
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury: Mariner 10 and MESSENGER; BepiColombo is en route.
Mercury has no moons and no rings.
Venus spins backward (retrograde), so the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.
A single rotation on Venus takes longer than its entire orbit around the Sun.
Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere creates a runaway greenhouse effect reaching 465°C.
Surface atmospheric pressure on Venus is 92 times Earth's—like being 900 meters underwater.
Venus is the brightest natural object in Earth's night sky after the Moon.
Its clouds are made of sulfuric acid droplets that reflect about 70% of sunlight.
Venus has more volcanoes than any other planet in the Solar System.
The Soviet Venera 13 lander survived for 127 minutes on the scorching surface in 1982.
Because of its similar size and mass, Venus is often called Earth's twin.
Upper cloud decks whip around the planet in just 4 Earth days.
Venus has no intrinsic global magnetic field.
Maxwell Montes, Venus's highest mountain, rises 11 km above the mean surface.
Earth is the only known world with liquid surface water and life.
About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by oceans.
Earth's magnetic field shields the atmosphere from being stripped away by the solar wind.
Plate tectonics constantly recycle Earth's crust, building mountains and ocean trenches.
Our 23.4° axial tilt is what gives Earth its changing seasons.
Earth's atmosphere is 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% argon and trace gases.
Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System at 5.51 grams per cubic centimeter.
The planet travels around the Sun at an average speed of 107,000 km/h.
Earth's rotation is gradually slowing by about 1.7 milliseconds per century due to lunar tides.
The Kármán line, 100 km above sea level, is the widely used boundary of space.
Earth is slightly flattened at the poles and bulges at the equator.
From space, city lights trace coastlines, rivers, and major highways across the night side.
The Moon is tidally locked to Earth, so we always see the same near side.
It is drifting away from Earth at about 3.8 centimeters per year.
The Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago, likely after a Mars-sized body struck early Earth.
Its gravitational pull is the primary driver of Earth's ocean tides.
The dark plains on the Moon, called maria, are ancient solidified lava flows.
Moon gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's—a 60 kg person weighs 10 kg there.
Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972 during the Apollo program.
Without an atmosphere, footprints left on the lunar dust can last millions of years.
A full lunar phase cycle (new moon to new moon) takes 29.5 days.
The South Pole–Aitken basin is one of the largest known impact craters in the Solar System.
The Moon stabilizes Earth's axial tilt, helping keep our climate relatively steady.
Lunar regolith is fine, sharp-edged rock dust created by billions of micrometeorite impacts.
Mars gets its rusty red color from iron oxide (rust) covering its surface.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano in the Solar System—nearly three times Mount Everest.
Valles Marineris is a canyon system over 4,000 km long, dwarfing the Grand Canyon.
A Martian day (a 'sol') is only 39 minutes longer than an Earth day.
Mars has two small, irregularly shaped moons: Phobos and Deimos.
Planet-wide dust storms can engulf Mars for months at a time.
Ancient river deltas and lakebeds prove liquid water once flowed on Mars.
Its thin atmosphere is 95% carbon dioxide and less than 1% as dense as Earth's.
Sunsets on Mars appear blue because fine dust scatters red light.
Mars has polar ice caps made of both water ice and frozen carbon dioxide (dry ice).
NASA's Ingenuity helicopter achieved the first powered flight on another planet in 2021.
Phobos orbits so close to Mars that it rises in the west and sets in the east.
Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.
It has the shortest day of any planet, spinning once in under 10 hours.
The Great Red Spot is a colossal storm larger than Earth that has raged for centuries.
Jupiter has no solid surface; its hydrogen atmosphere transitions into liquid metallic hydrogen.
Its four largest moons—Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto—were discovered by Galileo in 1610.
Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System, even bigger than Mercury.
Europa hides a global salty ocean beneath its icy crust.
Jupiter's magnetic field is 14 times stronger than Earth's, creating intense radiation belts.
Jupiter has a faint ring system made mostly of dust kicked up from small inner moons.
Io is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System due to Jupiter's tidal pull.
Jupiter acts as a gravitational shield, deflecting or capturing many incoming comets.
Stunning polar cyclones arranged in geometric patterns were revealed by NASA's Juno spacecraft.
Saturn's iconic rings span 282,000 km across yet are often less than 10 meters thick.
The rings are made of billions of chunks of water ice and rock.
Saturn is the only planet less dense than liquid water.
A persistent six-sided hexagonal jet stream swirls around Saturn's north pole.
Titan, Saturn's largest moon, has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane.
Enceladus shoots towering geysers of water ice from a subsurface ocean into space.
Saturn casts a sharp shadow across its own rings, and the rings cast bands of shadow on the globe.
Winds in Saturn's upper atmosphere can reach 1,800 km/h.
Saturn has more confirmed moons than any other planet in the Solar System.
The Cassini spacecraft orbited Saturn for 13 years before plunging into its atmosphere in 2017.
Saturn's rings are relatively young—possibly only 100 to 400 million years old.
Because of its rapid spin, Saturn is noticeably flattened at the poles.
Uranus rotates on its side with an axial tilt of 98 degrees, rolling around the Sun.
Each pole experiences 42 continuous years of sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.
Methane gas in its upper atmosphere absorbs red light, giving Uranus its pale cyan hue.
Uranus is an 'ice giant' composed mostly of water, ammonia, and methane ices.
It was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781.
Uranus has 13 known faint, dark rings.
It holds the record for the coldest planetary atmosphere measured, dipping to -224°C.
Its moons are named after characters from William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have flown past Uranus, in January 1986.
Uranus radiates very little internal heat compared to the other giant planets.
Its magnetic field is tilted 59 degrees from its spin axis and offset from the planet's center.
Like Venus, Uranus rotates in the retrograde direction.
Neptune was the first planet found by mathematical prediction before being seen in 1846.
It has the fastest sustained winds in the Solar System, exceeding 2,100 km/h.
Neptune completed its first full orbit since discovery in 2011—165 Earth years later.
Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backward and is likely a captured Kuiper Belt object.
Triton has active nitrogen geysers erupting across its frozen surface.
Neptune is 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth; sunlight there is 900 times dimmer.
It has six faint, dusty rings with bright clumpy arcs.
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to visit Neptune, flying by in August 1989.
Neptune radiates 2.6 times more energy than it receives from the Sun.
High-altitude methane ice clouds cast shadows on the deeper blue cloud deck below.
Neptune is slightly smaller than Uranus in diameter but more massive and denser.
A day on Neptune lasts just over 16 hours.
